**Wednesday, February 20, 1952**

You arrived on a Wednesday, fourteen days into the reign of a brand-new queen. King George VI had died in his sleep on February 6th — a shock to Britain and the Commonwealth — and a twenty-five-year-old Elizabeth II had been proclaimed monarch while she was still in Kenya on a wildlife tour. She wouldn't be crowned for another fifteen months, but the Elizabethan era had already begun. That queen would preside over the world for the next seventy years. You were born at its very start and outlived her by four.

---

**The world you entered**

The Korean War was seven months into a military stalemate that would grind on for another seventeen months. Peace talks had begun but repeatedly collapsed. American and Chinese forces were dug into positions neither side could break, and the front had barely moved in a year. Nearly three years of war had already killed millions — soldiers and civilians alike — and the outcome was still genuinely uncertain. A child born in February 1952 grew up in a country where that war was simply background noise, a low hum of casualty lists that never quite resolved.

Beneath it was a deeper anxiety. The Soviet Union had tested its first atomic bomb in 1949. Both superpowers now had the weapon. The hydrogen bomb — a thousand times more powerful — was still months away from its first American test, but the race was understood. The children of 1952 would grow up practicing nuclear drills, crouching under school desks, absorbing the idea that the world could end on a Tuesday afternoon.

Television had reached roughly a third of American homes by early 1952, but the medium was still finding itself. Most households got their news from radio and their entertainment from both. The culture was on the hinge between the old world and the broadcast one.

---

**The date itself has company across history**

Ten years before you were born, on February 20, 1942, a twenty-seven-year-old Navy lieutenant named Edward "Butch" O'Hare flew his Wildcat fighter alone into a formation of nine Japanese bombers bearing down on the aircraft carrier Lexington. In roughly four minutes, he shot down five of them and drove off the rest, saving the ship and the lives of hundreds of men. He was awarded the Medal of Honor — the Navy's first of the war — and when Chicago rebuilt its airport after the war, they named it for him. Everyone who has ever flown through O'Hare International is, in some distant way, still paying that debt. You arrived exactly a decade after his finest ten minutes.

---

**Your tenth birthday**

On February 20, 1962 — the day you turned ten — John Glenn climbed into a capsule called Friendship 7 and became the first American to orbit the Earth. He circled the globe three times in under five hours. The country had been losing the space race; Yuri Gagarin had orbited almost a year earlier. Glenn's flight didn't erase that gap, but it changed something in the national mood. The decade of your childhood ended with Americans walking on the Moon. You were seventeen when Neil Armstrong stepped off the ladder.

---

**Your thirty-fourth birthday**

On February 20, 1986, the Soviet Union launched the core module of Mir — the space station that would remain in orbit for fifteen years. You turned thirty-four the same day a new era of permanent human presence in space quietly began. Mir would host 125 cosmonauts and astronauts before it was deorbited in 2001, and it represented both the last great achievement of the Soviet space program and the first template for international cooperation in orbit that led directly to the ISS.

---

**The arc**

You are 74 years old now. The span of that lifetime is almost impossible to compress without losing something.

You were born before commercial television reached most homes, before the polio vaccine, before the first commercial jet passenger service, before the interstate highway system existed, before rock and roll had a name. The world held 2.5 billion people. Computing meant rooms full of vacuum tubes accessible to almost no one.

Over the decades that followed: the civil rights movement, the Kennedy assassination, Vietnam, the moon landing, the fall of the Berlin Wall, the collapse of the Soviet Union, the internet, 9/11, the smartphone, the mapping of the human genome, and now artificial intelligence producing fluent text and images at scales no one in 1952 would have found remotely plausible.

You entered a world where a long-distance phone call was an event, where you wrote letters and waited weeks for a reply, where information traveled as fast as paper could be printed and trucked. You have lived into a world where most of human knowledge can be retrieved in seconds by a device that fits in a shirt pocket.

The queen who took the throne two weeks before you were born is gone. So is the Soviet Union that shadowed your entire childhood. The Korea that was frozen in military stalemate when you arrived is now two countries, one of them a nuclear power of its own. The computers that occupied whole buildings in 1952 now fit on your wrist and are smarter than the room-sized ones ever were.

It has been a remarkable seventy-four years to be alive.
